Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:28: He explains the matter of the blemish further, saying: "they act so that the blessings from above are not drawn down upon them, as it says, 'and He will restrain the heavens and there will be no rain.'" The meaning is that it is the way of the supernal heavens to bestow upon the world an abundance of goodness and mercy for the lower beings, and the Holy One, blessed be He, must restrain them from bestowing in their usual way, as it is written "and He will restrain the heavens" - through this, a certain blemish reaches the heavens, along the lines of what is explained in the Zohar (Balak 197a), on the verse (Song of Songs 1:8) "if you do not know, O fairest among women," that Malchut is called "Atzeret" [restraint/assembly], for she gathers in all the supernal flow that comes to her and restrains it, giving to the lower beings only drop by drop, because they are not worthy - his words, briefly: "and when it reaches her, all that she has gathered, she restrains, holds back, and delays, so that it descends only like dew, drop by drop. Why? Because she does not find faithfulness below as she finds it [above], where it is poured out on every side without delay, and she rejoices, and then they give her many gifts and largesse, one to another, and they do not hold it back from her at all; but the lower beings hold it back, and hold her back, and then she is 'Atzeret,' restraining, holding - certainly, as it were, she gives only the residue and no more" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:29: Along these lines, a blemish reaches the heavens in that they must restrain themselves contrary to their custom, and from this comes to them a kind of pain - like the parable of a generous man, accustomed to give freely of his money, who, if his hand is held back from giving, undoubtedly suffers pain. "And they do not act [upon Him]" - for the heavens take for themselves [what they need], being full, for their own purpose, with flow and blessing, and the complete blemish that reaches the lower beings is that they receive nothing at all; this is what is meant by "and they do not take to draw it down below" - certainly, "their blemish is His children's" - and this they caused to themselves.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:30: Further, "'Lo' spelled with a Vav, that the right is not included in the left" - now he explains the blemish that reaches above in another manner besides the one stated, saying that the right is not included in the left, so that the right is not included with the left to subdue judgment, because the lower beings separate the evil inclination from the good inclination. And he says, "so that blessings are not drawn down below" - he returns to the first explanation, for the two matters are one, and therefore he did not say "another matter" but "further" - meaning an additional point beyond what was said, and indeed it is so.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:31: Once a person knows that his situation is not like that of the other created beings among the seventy nations - for whom it makes no difference, whether they strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination or the reverse, since they did not accept the whole Torah upon themselves - but rather that Israel, who are called children of the Omnipresent and are called "Adam," as it is said (Ezekiel 34:31) "you are Adam," and were created in the supreme image, as it is said (Genesis 9:6) "in the image of God He made man" - whatever they do acts upon the supernal roots on account of the soul within them, and the good inclination and evil inclination are bestowed upon them from above, as is explained in the Zohar (Bereishit 49a), that these are the secret of the two arms; see there. And further there (ibid.), on the verse (Genesis 3:6) "and the woman saw that the tree was good for food" - therefore one must always fear lest he blemish himself, that is, his soul, by the withdrawal of the supernal light from it - this is [the meaning of] "His children's is their blemish." For even though "and He will restrain the heavens and there will be no rain" could refer to physical rain, that would make sense in years of famine, but if in years of plenty he sins, how could "and He will restrain the heavens" apply? Rather, certainly it refers to the withdrawal of the light of Torah from the souls below, for the Torah is compared to rain, as it is said (Deuteronomy 32:2) "my teaching shall drop like the rain," etc., as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Ta'anit 7a); and likewise in the Tikkunim: "rain is nothing but the flowing-forth of Torah."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:32: Likewise, one must fear lest he blemish above, as I explained, and therefore one must always strengthen the good inclination over the evil inclination. Besides this, one must strengthen the side of kindness and mercy over judgment, in the matter of the attributes of compassion and acts of kindness and the like, all of which stem from the good inclination, which is the side of kindness, and remove from his heart the attributes of cruelty, vengeance, anger, and envy, all of which are attributes stemming from the evil inclination, whose root is the root of judgment.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:33: The way a person acquires fear in his heart is by subduing the kelipot and strengthening the good inclination over the evil inclination; and this Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, taught us in the verse (Deuteronomy 10:12) "and now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear," for he said (ibid. 10:16) "and you shall circumcise the foreskin of your heart" - and it is known that the foreskin stems from the evil inclination; and since he called it "foreskin," we may understand that the evil inclination has the laws of a foreskin applied to it, namely, "three years it shall be as forbidden fruit to you" - and it is explained in the Tikkunim (10b) that these correspond to the three shells of the walnut.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:34: It is known that in order to eat the kernel of the walnut one must break the shells, and therefore the prophets, before attaining holiness, first had to break through the shell: (Ezekiel 1:4) "and I looked, and behold, a storm wind came out of the north" - this is one; "a great cloud" - two; "and a fire flashing up" - three; "and a brightness around it" - this is the fourth, thin shell that is eaten together with the walnut, and from within it the likeness of the four Chayot, the four "heads" found in the walnut.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:35: These three shells are likewise mentioned in the words of Elijah, as it is said (I Kings 19:11) "and behold, the Lord passed by, and a great and strong wind rending mountains and breaking rocks in pieces before the Lord - the Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake - the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, a fire - the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, a still, small voice." My teacher, peace be upon him, explains in the Sefer HaPardes that although there are ten kelipot, their roots are three, corresponding to the three shells of the walnut mentioned. From this we learn that although the qualities of the evil inclination are many, their root is threefold, and these are the three shells of the evil inclination in the heart, even though they are, in a sense, one, as will be explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:36: The first is pride, corresponding to the "great and strong wind," and without doubt pride is the root of all evil traits, as we shall elaborate, with the Lord's help, in its own Gate. And so it is explained in the Tikkunim (69b), that the heart is like the walnut, having shells and a foreskin - their words: "and the coarseness of a heart that rules over its own shells and is not broken - of it is said (Proverbs 16:5) 'every haughty heart is an abomination to the Lord,' and the Shechinah does not rest upon it, and from the side of the shells human beings are called 'of uncircumcised heart'" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:37: The second, corresponding to the hard shell of the walnut, is a person's stiff-neckedness, and therefore Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said (Deuteronomy 10:16) "and circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and stiffen your neck no more" - and this too is a quality stemming from pride.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:38: The third is a person's boiling over in anger and speaking harshly, and among these is his own boiling in the fire of the evil inclination to commit a transgression; this corresponds to the "fire flashing up," and this too is a quality stemming from pride - this is [the meaning of] "the coarseness of a heart that rules over its own shells," for the coarseness of heart has these three shells mentioned, all of which flow forth from it.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:39: I heard from the honored sage Rabbi Avraham HaLevi that this is why it is said of these three, "the Lord was not in the wind, the Lord was not in the earthquake, the Lord was not in the fire" - because the Shechinah does not dwell in these three; but in "a still, small voice" - there the King comes. So too is it explained in the Tikkunim (3b); and it is likewise the way of the members of an earthly king's palace to speak in a hushed manner, and one whose words are in a soft voice follows the paths of humility, and without doubt he cleaves to the King, as we shall write regarding humility, with the Lord's help.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:40: This is the aspect of inner fear: that a person should think that he is always before the King, and fear before Him, and not raise his voice before Him. This is what is explained in the Tikkunim (ibid.): "a still, small voice" - this is the Yud, though there it is expounded for another purpose; nevertheless, for our purposes, having explained above that the secret of fear is the Yud, we learn what is necessary for acquiring fear - namely, [speaking with] a still, small voice, and distancing oneself from the three shells of pride, which are the great wind, the earthquake, and the fire.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:41: It may be that this is what Solomon the king, peace be upon him, intended in saying (Proverbs 8:13) "the fear of the Lord is to hate evil; pride and arrogance and the way of evil and a perverse mouth I hate." For in order to merit the fear of the Lord, which is the good hidden away, the kernel of the walnut, one must break and crush the foreskin, which is the evil, and distance oneself from it so much that it becomes hated and repugnant to draw near to it; this is [the meaning of] "to hate evil," which is the kelipot, and the evil in general consists of these three - pride, arrogance, and the way of evil, etc. - these being the three shells of the walnut which I explained are the root of evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:42: Now, a person merits breaking these shells by abstaining from the pleasures of the world, all of which stem from the shells of the foreskin of the serpent and the evil inclination; this is [the meaning of] (Psalms 34:10) "fear the Lord, His holy ones, for there is no lack for those who fear Him." And the Ramban, peace be upon him, explains (portion of Kedoshim) that every expression of holiness is a person's abstinence and restraint from the desires of the world, and restraining his speech and the like; we shall quote his words, with the Lord's help, in the matters that lead to humility, one of which is holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:43: Likewise one must be careful of every negative commandment in the Torah, for whoever breaches the fence of a negative commandment causes the evil serpent to enter within; this is [the meaning of] "fearing God and turning away from evil" (Job 1:8). So too David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 34:12-15) "come, children, listen to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life, who loves days to see good? Guard your tongue from evil," etc., "turn away from evil and do good." And the reason he connects to fear "who is the man who desires life" is because the fear of the Lord is a source of life, as I explained above at the end of chapter 2.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:44: The matter of "turn away from evil and do good" is the fear explained by Rashbi, peace be upon him, in the passage we quoted above from the portion of Bereishit (7b), "because it is the tree of good and evil - if a person merits, behold, it is good; if he does not merit, behold, it is evil." Therefore it says "turn away from evil," meaning to distance oneself from evil to the utmost degree of distancing; and so Solomon the king, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 14:16) "a wise man fears and turns away from evil."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:45: The reason is as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Avot 4:2): "one mitzvah leads to another mitzvah, and one transgression leads to another transgression." The pious Rabbi Yosef Yaavetz explains this Mishnah: since the commandments stem from the Tree of Life and are spiritual things that cling to Him, blessed be He, one who performs a mitzvah cleaves to Him, blessed be He, and whoever adds more mitzvot adds more cleaving. If so, one mitzvah leads to another mitzvah, and the reward of a mitzvah is a mitzvah, along the lines of "one who sanctifies himself somewhat from below is sanctified greatly from above" - this is the summary of his intent. This is [the meaning of] "if a person merits, behold, it is good" - for the good to which he cleaves becomes his portion, and if, God forbid, he cleaves to evil, the evil becomes his portion, and he is destined to do much evil. So too the pious one, of blessed memory, explains there concerning "one who flees from transgression" - that fleeing means seeing before oneself a great blazing fire from which one must distance oneself as far as a bowshot. I found support for this interpretation in the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, quoted in the Yalkut (Mishlei, remez 959), on the verse (Proverbs 19:2) "also, without knowledge, the soul is not good, and one who hastens with his feet sins" - their words: "our Sages have taught: one mitzvah leads to another mitzvah, and one transgression leads to another transgression; a person should not grieve over transgressions he committed unintentionally, [but consider] that an opening has been made for him to sin even deliberately; and a person should not rejoice over a mitzvah that has come to his hand, [but consider] that many mitzvot are destined to come to his hand. Therefore, if a person sins unintentionally, of him it is said, 'and one who hastens with his feet sins'" - so far.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:46: This is the aspect of fear of sin: that one should distance himself from sin and fear it, for sin is the evil, the impurity and refuse of holiness, and it is an expression of deficiency, as in (I Kings 1:21) "I and my son Solomon will be counted as sinners [chata'im, deficient]," for the kelipot are deficient in the supernal light. For this reason, one must fear lest an opening be made for him to transgressions, for "this too, corresponding to that, God made" - just as one who performs mitzvot, the more he performs, the more he cleaves to the supernal spirituality, so one who commits transgressions cleaves to transgressions in such a way that he comes from unintentional sin to deliberate sin.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:47: As for the reason it says "if a person sins unintentionally, of him it is said, 'and one who hastens with his feet sins,'" this is along the lines of what our Sages, of blessed memory, said at the end of the third chapter of Yoma (39a) on "do not defile yourselves with them, lest you become defiled through them" (Leviticus 11:43): a person who defiles himself a little is defiled a great deal [from above]. So too, this matter is understood when we understand what they said there about holiness: a person who sanctifies himself a little is sanctified a great deal [from above].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:48: The matter is that the soul within man, and the matter of the Torah's commandments taking on physical form, follow one and the same pattern: for the soul within a person's body is constricted, similar to how the Holy One, blessed be He, constricted His Shechinah between the poles of the Ark - for above, the heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain Him, yet nevertheless, out of love for Israel and for their benefit, He constricted His Shechinah there. So too the matter of the soul: for above, before it was clothed in this world, it shines without limit, greater than the angels, since it is emanated and hewn from the Throne of Glory, as they say, "souls are hewn from the Throne of Glory"; and just as every level of the Throne is greater than everything beneath it, as we explained in chapter 2, so are the souls that derive from it. This is especially so if it is a soul of Atzilut, which shines more and more, and its light encompasses all that is below it; and we already know that the soul is compared to the Holy One, blessed be He - just as the Holy One, blessed be He, sees but is not seen, so too the souls, as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 10a). And they also said (Pesachim 8a): to what are the souls of the righteous, before the Shechinah, compared? To candles before a torch. From this we understand what is said in the Zohar (Emor 103b), that the souls of the Patriarchs, and Moses, Aaron, Joseph, and David, come to every sukkah of Israel - and how could this be conceived except along the lines stated? We find, then, that the soul in this coarse body of man is constricted contrary to its own nature.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:49: The same thing happened to the Torah and the commandments: for every single commandment, above, is a supernal light cleaving to the Tree of Life, since a mitzvah is YHVH, as is explained in the Tikkunim (131b) and Ra'aya Meheimna (Pinchas 228b). But through the sin of Adam, and likewise through the sin of the Golden Calf, the Torah and the commandments took on physical form, and a person now performs a physical mitzvah, such as wearing a tallit with tzitzit, or tefillin of leather, and the like for the other commandments; my teacher, peace be upon him, elaborated on this discourse in many places.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:50: So too, it is explained in the Tikkunim (4a) concerning the vowel points, that below they appear to us small, while above they shine without limit, like the sun, which appears small to us but is many times larger than the earth. And likewise, concerning the letters, it is explained in the portion of Acharei Mot (73a), that several worlds hang upon the thorn/point of the supernal Yud - their words: "one thousand four hundred and fifty myriad worlds all hang upon the point [tip] of the Alef, and other worlds hang upon the whole body of the Alef," see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:51: We find, then, that when a person now performs the physical mitzvah, and it seems to him a small thing, in the eyes of the Blessed Holy One it is very great - for in performing the physical mitzvah he arouses its spiritual root above, and the spirituality of that mitzvah above has no measure or limit, and therefore they said that he is sanctified above, greatly, without measure.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:52: Along these lines, it is explained in Chovot HaLevavot (Gate of Self-Reckoning, chapter 5) - his words: "and let no good deed you do for His Name seem small in your eyes, even a mere word or glance, for the little you give is much before Him; and likewise concerning transgressions. And the closest analogy for this is the movement of the sun over the earth - a span of a cubit's movement on earth corresponds to a movement of many miles on the celestial sphere; and so too the movement of the shadow on the astrolabe" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:53: With this we understand why the Blessed Holy One needed to give a person reward such that many thousands upon thousands of angels are appointed over each single mitzvah, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explains (Zohar, Pekudei 244b-262b) concerning the Holy Palaces. The reason is that the supernal light of the spirituality of that mitzvah sparkles forth through all those lesser palaces; and if you say, it should suffice for there to be one angel - we answer that it is impossible for the supernal light to sparkle within a single angel, for then that angel would be [equal to] the spirituality of the mitzvah itself in its own place, and would itself be the mitzvah, which is not the intent; rather, the light sparkles forth into vessels in which the soul may take delight, yet nonetheless there is one angel in whom the essential light of the mitzvah resides, and beneath him are several thousands who receive the remaining sparks of the light.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:54: From this we come to understand the matter of impurity: for when a person transgresses one commandment of our holy Torah, such as eating forbidden fat or blood or the like, this matter below is physical and appears to the transgressor a small thing, yet above it is impurity without measure - for according to the spiritual ascent of the mitzvah, so is the measure of the descent of impurity among the many angels of destruction. This is why it is explained that many bundles of impure spirits attach themselves to the soul, as it says regarding the palaces of impurity, several times (see Mikeitz 200a), and likewise several "guardians of laws" (263b, 265a); for the great impurity, which is the matter of that great judgment, must be divided among all those forces to judge the soul, so that it can receive its punishment through each and every one of them.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 4:55: We find, in this, a reason for a person to distance himself from evil, which is sin, and to fear lest it come to him even unintentionally, because of the disgrace of sin and the impurity within it; rather, he should cleave to the good, which is the good that endures forever and ever, so that it may be good for you forever, in the world that is entirely good, and in the world that is entirely long.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:1: This chapter will explain the modes of fear stemming from the blemish that reaches above, in the Shechinah, and [will discuss] distancing oneself from the enticements of the evil inclination, and drawing near to the good.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:2: Our Sages, of blessed memory, said, quoted in the Yalkut, portion of Chukat (remez 768), on the verse (Numbers 21:34) "and the Lord said to Moses, fear him not" - their words: "This is what Scripture says (Proverbs 28:14) 'happy is the man who fears always' - such is the way of the righteous: even though the Holy One, blessed be He, assures them, they do not cast off fear from themselves. So too it is written of Jacob (Genesis 32:8) 'and Jacob was greatly afraid' - why was he afraid? He said, perhaps I have become sullied in some way while with Laban; and it is written (Deuteronomy 23:15) 'and He shall see no unseemly thing among you and turn away from you' - and the Holy One, blessed be He, left me [i.e., protected me]. Moses too seized upon fear - why was he afraid? He said, perhaps Israel committed some trespass in the war against Sichon, or became sullied by transgression; He said to him, 'fear him not'" - so far, as relevant to us.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:3: According to the plain sense apparent from this passage: "and He shall see no unseemly thing among you" means no defect of any kind, that is, the sullying of some sin, "and turn away from you" - that the Shechinah would depart from him. And the question "why was he afraid" is understood by what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 4a), that Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction: it is written (Genesis 28:15) "and behold, I am with you, and I will keep you wherever you go," and it is written (32:8) "and Jacob was greatly afraid" - he feared lest sin be the cause; and the explanation of "lest sin be the cause" is along the lines of "perhaps I have become sullied in some way while with Laban," and it is written, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:4: However, in the Zohar (Acharei Mot 75a-b) it explains that "unseemly thing" [ervat davar] refers to the Shechinah - his words: "Rabbi Shimon opened: 'for the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp to save you,' etc. (Deuteronomy 23:15) - for the Lord your God, this is the Shechinah that is found among Israel, and how much more so in exile, to protect them always from every side and from all the other idol-worshiping nations, that they should not destroy Israel; for we are taught that the wicked among Israel cannot harm them until the wicked among Israel weaken the power of the Shechinah before the great ministering princes of the other nations - then the wicked among Israel are able to rule over them and decree upon them many evil decrees. And when they repent and return to receive her [the Shechinah], she breaks the power and strength of all those great ministering princes and breaks the power and strength of the wicked among Israel and exacts payment from all. And therefore, 'and your camp shall be holy,' for a person must not defile himself with his sins and transgress the words of the Torah - for if he does so, they defile him, as it is written (Leviticus 11:43) 'venitmetem bam' [without an Aleph, implying an intensified defilement]. And we learn that there are two hundred and forty-eight limbs in the body, and they are all defiled when he is defiled - that is, when he seeks to defile himself - and therefore, 'and your camp shall be holy' - what is 'your camp'? These are the limbs of the body - 'and He shall see no unseemly thing among you' - the nakedness of this 'thing,' as we have established; for if it were otherwise, then certainly 'and turn away from you.' And this is why it is written 'you shall not uncover the nakedness of your father's wife' - why? Because it is written 'it is your father's nakedness,' as we have established."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:5: We learn: for three things Israel is delayed in exile - because they treat the Shechinah with contempt in exile, and turn their faces away from the Shechinah, and because they defile themselves before the Shechinah; and all of this we have established in our teaching - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:6: Now, in general, four aspects concerning the blemish are mentioned in this passage. The first: when Israel sins, they weaken the power of the Shechinah before the seventy [heavenly] princes, and this is the Shechinah's complaint (Song of Songs 1:6) "they made me keeper of the vineyards" - these being the seventy princes - "my own vineyard," which is Israel, "I have not kept." And therefore it says (Deuteronomy 23:15) "for the Lord your God walks in the midst of your camp to save you and to deliver your enemies before you," etc.; but when a person causes a blemish, she does not save, but rather, God forbid, it is said of her (ibid. 32:18) "the Rock that bore you, you have weakened," as our Sages, of blessed memory, explained, which I quoted in chapter 3.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:7: Along these lines, Rashbi, peace be upon him, said (Vayetze 152b), on the verse (Proverbs 24:10) "if you slacken on the day of distress, your strength is limited [tzar kochacha]" - his words: "'if you slacken' - if he releases his hands from the Torah; 'on the day of distress, your strength is limited' - what is 'tzar kochacha'? It constricts the power of the Heh [i.e., diminishes the power of the divine attribute represented by that letter], for it is always at the right hand, and its protection is always upon a person when he walks in the ways of the Torah, and then it pushes the evil away, so that it cannot draw near to the person and cannot accuse him. But when a person strays from the ways of the Torah and slackens from it, then it 'constricts the power of the Heh,' because the evil, which is on the left, rules over the person and pushes this Heh outward, until it forces it into a place of distress" - so far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:8: The second and third aspects concerning the blemish are "and your camp shall be holy" and "and He shall see no unseemly thing among you." The matter is that when a person causes a blemish above, he darkens that light in the aspect of the limb with which he blemished, and mercy withdraws from there and judgment prevails; therefore this blemish must be transferred downward, whether by afflicting him with sufferings in his body or his money, or that darkness and judgment is kept in store to be transferred to his soul, in that it will enter the fire of Gehinnom and there be refined and receive all that judgment in the measure of his blemish; this is [the meaning of] (Leviticus 24:20) "as he has caused a blemish in a man, so shall it be done to him" - and "man" [Adam] here is the supernal Adam.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:9: Now, in order to arouse a person to repent, they defile him and place a blemish upon him corresponding to the nakedness and the blemish he blemished in the "thing" that is the Shechinah - this is [the meaning of] "it shall not be seen in you," meaning the blemish and the nakedness you blemished in the "thing" shall not be visible in your body; rather, "and your camp shall be holy" - that all his two hundred and forty-eight limbs should be holy, meaning all of them unified as one, so that we can say of them that they are all together, as one single limb, holy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:10: The matter is that when a person blemishes even one limb, it is considered as though he blemished the entire body, since all two hundred and forty-eight limbs are unified as one; therefore, even though he sinned in only one limb, all his two hundred and forty-eight limbs are defiled. This is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, said: "two hundred and forty-eight limbs in one body, and they are all defiled."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 5:11: With this we understand, in a second way, what our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 39a): "a person who defiles himself a little is defiled a great deal" - meaning that even though he sinned in only one limb, all his two hundred and forty-eight limbs are defiled greatly. And likewise concerning "and your camp shall be holy": "one who sanctifies himself a little is sanctified a great deal" - for even though he sanctified only one limb, all two hundred and forty-eight limbs, which are "your camp" in the plural, are sanctified with supernal holiness - "holy" in the singular, as I explained - as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (see Kiddushin 39b), "one who performs a mitzvah as it should be performed merits the life of the World to Come."
